description: The standard rule's file set: which files RetroArch writes for a core on a system, declared from the frontend's naming rule and the core's own source rather than read off the save directory. Three things these vectors pin. That the answer is a DECLARATION: a file lying under the content's stem which this core cannot write is not reported, because it is evidence about the past and the question is where this configuration writes now. That a record is keyed by core AND system: one mGBA answers a Game Boy cartridge's clock and a Game Boy Advance cartridge's not at all, so the same core states different sets for its two systems and states nothing at all where the system is unknown. And that the claim is pinned to the build it was read at, because a rebuild is exactly what can add or drop a memory id. A core with no record keeps the old answer — the directory resolves and the file set stays what it always was.

vectors.name: a-standard-core-names-the-save-before-one-exists
vectors.rationale: The question this family answers: where and under what name does this configuration write, with nothing in the save directory yet. mGBA on Game Boy Advance fills only the save-RAM id, so the answer is one name, declared from the frontend's naming rule and the core's own source — not a look at the directory.

vectors.name: a-clock-cartridge-core-names-both-files
vectors.rationale: Gambatte offers the frontend both memory ids, so both names belong in the candidate set — the Game Boy games that carry a clock write the second one. The set is an upper bound over the system, never a claim that this cartridge has the hardware.

vectors.name: a-file-left-behind-does-not-become-the-answer
vectors.rationale: The whole reason this answer is a declaration. A .rtc lies in the save directory under the content's own stem — left by a different core, or by this one before the arrangement changed. mGBA on Game Boy Advance cannot write it, and the answer says so instead of reporting what is lying there: a file on disk is evidence about the past, and this question is about where the configuration writes now.

vectors.name: one-core-two-systems-answers-each-on-its-own-terms
vectors.rationale: mGBA is the reason a record is keyed by core AND system: the same binary answers a Game Boy cartridge's clock and a Game Boy Advance cartridge's not at all. Asked for the Game Boy entry, the same core states the pair.

vectors.name: without-a-system-the-file-set-stays-unknown
vectors.rationale: The direct route is handed a core and nothing else. mGBA's two systems disagree about the clock file, so narrowing to one of them would be a guess — the set stays unknown and the directory answer stands on its own.

vectors.name: a-rebuilt-core-reopens-the-claim
vectors.rationale: The drift tripwire. Which memory ids a core fills is exactly what a new build can change, so the claim is pinned to the build it was read at and a machine running another one gets it with unverified-version beside it rather than inheriting it unexamined.

vectors.name: an-unrecorded-core-states-no-file-set
vectors.rationale: A core absent from the records is not one that writes nothing — it is one whose source nobody has read. The directory still resolves; the file set is the honest unknown, and the answer never fills the gap from what happens to lie there.

vectors.name: an-unreadable-core-earns-no-claim-from-its-file-name
vectors.rationale: A record is read out of one build's source. Where the installed core cannot be examined at all, applying it on the strength of the .so file name would state a source-verified claim about a binary nobody read — the decision the rule-card path already makes in the same state. The directory still resolves; the file set does not.

vectors.name: a-directory-that-cannot-be-listed-does-not-degrade-a-declaration
vectors.rationale: The save directory refuses to be listed. For a recorded core that changes nothing: the names follow from the naming rule and the core's source, neither of which is on that disk, so the answer stands and carries no unlistable caveat — reporting one would degrade something this question no longer asks.

vectors.name: a-core-that-fills-no-memory-id-says-so-and-says-what-stays-open
vectors.rationale: The commonest shape once the reading starts: blueMSX answers no libretro memory id, so RetroArch writes it no save file at all. That is a declared emptiness, not an unknown — atlas looked. And it is deliberately not the whole story: MSX games do have battery and disk saves, an emulator can keep them past the frontend, and the caveat says that half is unestablished so nobody reads 'no files' as 'nothing to back up'. No granularity travels with it: there is no save here to group. (This vector rode on DeSmuME until its read established the core's own .dsv and a card replaced the record.)

vectors.name: a-handheld-that-does-use-the-interface-still-names-its-file
vectors.rationale: The other outcome from the same batch, so the two are pinned side by side: Arduous answers RETRO_MEMORY_SAVE_RAM with the Arduboy's EEPROM size, so the frontend writes one file and the answer names it.

vectors.name: a-cartridge-with-battery-ram-names-one-file-across-ten-systems
vectors.rationale: Genesis Plus GX is the busiest core on the default list: it is what RetroDECK launches for ten systems, from Mega Drive to Game Gear, and it fills the save-RAM id on every one of them. One record, ten entries, one name per game — and no .rtc, because the core has no clock branch at all.

vectors.name: a-clock-only-a-few-cartridges-carry-still-belongs-in-the-set
vectors.rationale: Snes9x offers the frontend both memory ids, and the clock one answers a size only while the loaded cartridge drives S-RTC or the SPC7110 clock — a handful of games out of a library. The set is an upper bound over the system, so both names are stated: atlas does not read cartridges, and a caller looking for the second file finds it where it would be. One record serves every flavour of the machine the catalogue declares.

vectors.name: a-second-choice-core-answers-with-its-own-reading
vectors.rationale: A frontend offers several emulators per system and a user picks one — for an arcade library that is routinely not the one the catalogue leads with. The record describes the core, not the position it holds in a menu, so the second entry answers from the same reading. DICE fills no memory id, so the answer is a declared emptiness with the rest of the story left open, exactly as it is on the system this core does lead. It took this case over from FB Alpha 2012, which turned out to write past the frontend after all and now carries a card — and a card is the opposite of the emptiness this vector is about.

vectors.name: a-second-choice-core-names-files-where-it-fills-the-interface
vectors.rationale: The other half of the same rule, with names rather than an emptiness. PicoDrive is the catalogue's second offer for Mega Drive and fills the save-RAM id, so choosing it states the file the frontend writes — a system a core does not lead is not a system atlas knows less about.

vectors.name: three-trees-one-save-and-one-of-them-cannot-be-named
vectors.rationale: MAME answers no libretro memory id and still saves plenty — in three directories of its own. The battery memory is the save, the dip switches beside it are settings, and the emulator-wide default.cfg in the same directory belongs to every machine at once: three groups, two roles, two groupings, so a client can take the progress and leave the configuration. The fourth tree is the honest hole. MAME names a hard disk's differencing image after the disk's entry in the machine's own ROM table, which is no read of this machine — upstream calls the scheme unscalable on the line that builds it — so the answer names the directory and refuses the file names rather than guessing them, because a backup that skips it loses the progress of every machine with a hard disk.

data.files_established_for: content whose file stem is spelled exactly as MAME spells the driver. running_machine takes its basename straight from the driver (machine.cpp:74, m_basename(_config.gamedrv().name)) and every name below is built on it, while the glue finds the driver from the content's basename (retro_init.cpp:285-305). For a MAME-conformant romset the two are the same string; for a collection that spells its files otherwise, the stem here is right up to case.
data.citation: machine.cpp:74 and :1116-1147 at libretro/mame a90e86e1

romload.cpp:1111-1123 at libretro/mame a90e86e1 — the differencing image for a CHD hard disk is named after the disk image's own entry in the machine's ROM table inside the binary (romp->name() + ".dif"), which is no read of this machine. Upstream says so on the line above it: 'TODO: use system name and/or software list name in the path - the current setup doesn't scale'. The same directory is used by a mounted hard disk image (harddriv.cpp:196-200).

vectors.name: a-core-that-keeps-its-saves-in-a-subtree-of-its-own-says-so
vectors.rationale: FinalBurn Neo answers no libretro memory id, and that is not the same as writing nothing: it keeps a driver's battery memory in a directory of its own below the save root. The card states the subtree, the file, what kind of data it is and whom it belongs to — and which option decides that, read live, with what the other values would mean. In the registered default no memory card exists at all, so the answer is one file and one group.

vectors.name: a-second-choice-core-that-is-not-one-behaviour-answers-gb-on-its-own-terms
vectors.rationale: VBA-M is the catalogue's alternative for both Game Boy and Game Boy Advance, and its memory function switches on the loaded image type before answering: the Game Boy branch has a clock case, the Game Boy Advance branch has none. So the same core states two files for one of its systems and one for the other — the second core in the records to do that, and the reason they are keyed by core *and* system rather than by core alone.

vectors.name: a-second-choice-core-that-is-not-one-behaviour-answers-gba-on-its-own-terms
vectors.rationale: VBA-M is the catalogue's alternative for both Game Boy and Game Boy Advance, and its memory function switches on the loaded image type before answering: the Game Boy branch has a clock case, the Game Boy Advance branch has none. So the same core states two files for one of its systems and one for the other — the second core in the records to do that, and the reason they are keyed by core *and* system rather than by core alone.

vectors.name: the-fifth-emulator-a-system-offers-answers-like-the-first
vectors.rationale: Game Boy is the first system whose whole emulator list answers. The catalogue offers five libretro cores for it and a person scrolling that list is as likely to stop at the last as at the first, so the last one is what this asks: DoubleCherryGB fills both memory ids and states the same pair of names Gambatte states from position one. Position in a menu is not a property of a core, and it is not a reason for atlas to know less.

vectors.name: the-one-ds-core-that-uses-the-interface-names-its-file
vectors.rationale: Every Nintendo DS core read before this one answers no memory id at all — DeSmuME keeps its save past the frontend and so do its siblings — so the honest answer for the system has been an empty set or an unknown. melonDS DS is the exception: it answers the save-RAM id with the save manager's own length, so RetroArch writes the file and the answer names it. One system, four emulators, and which one is chosen decides whether a file with that name exists at all.

vectors.name: an-older-arcade-build-keeps-three-trees-and-names-all-of-them
vectors.rationale: MAME 2000 is the catalogue's second offer for arcade and it saves the way its generation did: three directories of its own below the save directory, every file named after the driver. All three are nameable, so nothing is refused here — which is what makes it the counterpart to the current MAME's answer, where one tree cannot be listed. The score table is its own role: a machine keeps one for everyone who ever played it, and merging two of them is not the same operation as merging two battery saves.

data.files_established_for: content whose file stem is spelled exactly as MAME spells the driver. The file is named after the driver, not after the ROM file: MAME 2000 matches the content's basename against its driver table case-insensitively (libretro.c:862-871, and a miss refuses the load), and then writes the table's own spelling. For a MAME-conformant romset the two are the same string; for a collection that spells its files otherwise, the stem here is right up to case.

vectors.name: an-arcade-build-states-two-directories-it-cannot-list
vectors.rationale: MAME 2010 is the first answer with two directories whose file names atlas cannot derive, and the reason differs for each: a memory card is named after an index the player picks in the emulator's own interface, a differencing image after a disk's entry in the machine's ROM table. Both are groups like any other — directory, granularity and role stated, only the list refused — so one walk over groups reaches all six places this save lives. The memory cards are shared-card besides: one directory holds every card the machine ever made, so restoring one game's copy would overwrite every other game's.

vectors.name: a-core-whose-options-a-probe-cannot-reach-still-answers-from-its-own-default
vectors.rationale: MAME 2003 puts its whole save tree under a subfolder or directly under the save directory, and an option decides which. That option is one a probe of the shipped binary cannot see — the core registers its options later than a probe reaches — so nothing on this machine states the value. The card records the default the core's own source declares, which is what a recorded default is for: it is kept only for a core that registers none, so it can never become a second, ageing copy of something the machine already says. The answer is the subfolder, and the alternative is named beside it with the value that would reach it.

vectors.name: an-arcade-core-whose-score-table-is-a-second-file-behind-an-option
vectors.rationale: FB Alpha keeps the non-volatile half of a machine's state in <driver>.fs, and where its hiscore option is on it keeps the score table beside it in <driver>.hi. Two files, two roles, one directory — and the second only exists because a switch says so, which is why the option governs the file set rather than merely appearing next to it. The option is on here through the frontend's own core-options file; this build ships with it off.

data.files_established_for: content whose file stem is the driver's own name. FB Alpha names the file after the loaded driver, and its lookup is exact: BurnDrvGetIndexByName compares with strcmp, so a content basename that differs from the driver name in any way — case included — refuses to load at all. Where the game runs, the two strings are equal.
data.citation: src/burner/libretro/libretro.cpp:1429 (write) and :2899 (read) at libretro/fbalpha2012_neogeo fa3bf50

vectors.name: a-ds-core-that-writes-past-the-frontend-still-names-its-file
vectors.rationale: Three of the four emulators a Nintendo DS library offers keep their save past the frontend, and until now each answered with a declared emptiness and an open half. melonDS is the first of them read far enough to close it: the core builds <save_dir>/<rom_stem>.sav itself and hands that path to the emulator, so the answer names the file rather than saying no file exists. Same directory a frontend-written save would have used, different writer.

vectors.name: a-handheld-whose-save-name-replaces-the-content-extension
vectors.rationale: RACE keeps the Neo Geo Pocket's flash memory itself, and it builds the name by replacing the content file's extension rather than appending to a stem. The result is the same string for ordinary content, which is why the answer states <rom_stem>.ngf — but the route matters for one case the card records: content whose whole path carries no dot gets no save file at all.

vectors.name: four-files-for-one-game-and-one-of-them-shares-the-frontends-name
vectors.rationale: Geolith writes four files of its own per game — the board's NVRAM, the cartridge RAM, a memory card and the CD backup RAM — into the frontend's own save directory. Three roles across four names, so a client can tell the memory card from the rest. The second name is why this is a card and not a record: for CD content the core also fills the save-RAM id, so RetroArch writes <rom_stem>.srm onto the same path the core writes at unload. Every other two-writer case read so far kept the two apart by name. The answer states the set either way, because the names are the core's and it writes them for cartridge content too.

vectors.name: the-last-emulator-a-system-offers-completes-it
vectors.rationale: Game Boy Advance is offered by five emulators and this is the fifth. Four of them fill the libretro save interface and RetroArch writes their file; NooDS fills none of it and keeps a <rom_stem>.sav of its own, opened as a descriptor the emulator writes into directly. Same directory, different writer, and with it every emulator the system offers answers — the fourth system to reach that, after Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Super Game Boy. The file is also created on first launch whether the game ever saves or not, which the card records and the answer does not need to: the set is what can be written, and this one always is.

vectors.name: a-save-that-is-nothing-but-score-tables
vectors.rationale: Cannonball is a port of one arcade game, and everything it keeps is a score table: three of them, for the game's three modes, under fixed names that follow nothing about the content. So the whole save is one group with the high-score role and shared-file granularity — the first shipped card where that is the entire answer rather than one part of it. A client syncing saves takes them, because the rule is every role but settings; a client that reads the role knows to merge the higher entries rather than overwrite with the newer file, which is the only case where that distinction changes what to do.

vectors.name: a-per-content-directory-keyed-by-the-contents-stem
vectors.rationale: prboom answers no libretro memory id and creates a directory of its own under the frontend's save root, named after the content's stem — the card's subdir is the template <rom_stem>, filled by the resolver from the content path. Everything inside is nameable: eight menu-slot savegames (role battery, scoped by the DeHackEd caveat because a .deh may rename their base) and a written-back prboom.cfg (role settings) share the one directory, so the flat list is their concatenation and the roles keep a save sync from carrying the config.

data.citation: d_deh.c:492 sets the base to 'prbmsav'; :840 lists SAVEGAMENAME among the strings a .deh may replace, and the loader passes a matching .deh found beside the content (libretro.c:2399, :2611)

vectors.name: a-per-content-directory-keyed-by-the-directorys-name
vectors.rationale: The vitaquake2 family keys its directory by the basename of the content's directory — the card's subdir is the template <content_dir_name>, and for content in baseq2/ the save root gains a baseq2/ of its own. Inside it the two kinds part ways: config.cfg is nameable (role settings, shared by everything that shares the directory), while Quake 2's save/ slot tree holds per-map level states whose names follow the maps the player visited — so that group states the directory, refuses the names, and the file-names-unestablished caveat carries the reason.

data.citation: Quake 2's slot layout below it: while playing, every level crossed writes save/current/<map>.sav and <map>.sv2 (sv_init.c:193, :206); a save copies them into save/<slot>/ beside a server.ssv and game.ssv (sv_ccmds.c:219-227). The per-map names follow the maps the player visited and the slot set is open ('current', 'quick', 'save0' on up), which is nothing atlas reads

vectors.name: a-card-rooted-in-the-contents-own-tree
vectors.rationale: boom3 hands its engine the ROM tree as the save path and never writes into the directory it builds under the frontend's save root — so the card's root is content_directory, and the answer lives beside the content: a written-back libretro.cfg (role settings) and the savegames/ subtree whose user-typed names atlas cannot derive (files null, role battery, with the file-names-unestablished caveat carrying the reason). The live check that prompted this vector caught the resolver answering the save root for exactly this card, because no earlier card had ever used the content root.

data.citation: Doom 3 names a savegame after what the player typed into the save dialog, scrubbed, with a .tga preview and a .txt description beside it (framework/Session.cpp:2236-2249) — three files per save under names that are nothing atlas reads

vectors.name: a-save-whose-directory-is-the-launchs-own
vectors.rationale: DeSmuME 2015 composes its save path from a variable its libretro build never fills, so <rom_stem>.dsv (and the .dsv.bak the core makes before overwriting) lands relative to the working directory of whatever process loaded the core. That is a property of the launch, not of the machine, so the answer's root is working_directory: dir is the <cwd> template, needs carries the cwd hole only the launcher can fill, the file names are stated anyway — the reading is not wasted — and the save-dir-launch-dependent caveat carries the sentence. Nothing on the machine is read for a template: no observation, no link view, no fallback.

vectors.name: a-cd-system-where-the-interface-claim-was-unreachable
vectors.rationale: Genesis Plus GX really fills save_ram — for cartridges. On the CD systems that code is unreachable: SYSTEM_MCD initializes the CD hardware instead of the cartridge hardware, sram.on never sets, and the memory interface answers 0, so RetroArch writes nothing. The record's megacd rows used to claim save_ram anyway, citing the reachable memory switch without tracing which systems reach it — the audit's first wrong shipped row. This vector pins the corrected answer: a declared set of no files, with core-own-writes-unestablished carrying what that outcome cannot settle. What the core does write there — its BRAM tree under three interacting options — is the multi-option card work the audit queue carries.

vectors.name: a-quake-port-keyed-by-the-contents-directory
vectors.rationale: tyrquake answers no libretro memory id and joins the frontend's save directory with the basename of the content's directory — for the usual layout <base>/id1/pak0.pak that is 'id1', kept even when the engine re-roots its basedir one level up. Inside, everything is nameable: Quake's twelve menu-slot savegames s0.sav-s11.sav (role battery, scoped because the console's save command takes a free name) beside a written-back config.cfg (role settings), so the flat list is their concatenation and the roles keep a save sync from carrying the config.

vectors.name: a-sorted-root-hole-keeps-the-cards-subdir
vectors.rationale: Content sorting with no content named leaves a hole in the base directory — which withholds every observation, not the card's subtree: the core appends its subdirectory to whatever GET_SAVE_DIRECTORY hands it, sorted or not. The answer must carry both template segments with both holes; stating the parent as the final directory was the wiring the live check caught.

vectors.name: a-disk-diff-that-spells-the-frontends-name
vectors.rationale: quasi88 answers no save memory id, and with its governing option at the registered default it keeps a differencing file per opened disk image as <save dir>/<image stem>.srm — created empty at launch, byte differences on write, the image untouched. The name spells exactly what the frontend would write for a core that fills save_ram, without the frontend writing anything, which is why only the card can say whose file it is. The declared name is scoped: an .m3u playlist's members and anything the core's own menu opens bring their own stems.

data.files_established_for: content loaded as a single disk image. Every disk the core opens gets a differencing file named after that image's own stem — an .m3u playlist's member images each bring theirs, and the core's built-in menu can open further images with theirs
data.citation: src/LIBRETRO/file-op.c:252-254 at libretro/quasi88-libretro 42be798 — the diff is named after the opened image's basename; libretro.c:684-685 inserts the content path, load_m3u (:616-670) appends each playlist member, menu.c:2469 opens what the menu picks

vectors.name: an-option-that-moves-the-writes-into-the-image-itself
vectors.rationale: The first card whose two modes stand on different roots: quasi88's q88_save_to_disk_image enabled abandons the differencing file and writes the sectors into the loaded .d88 itself — the save is the modified content file, and the answer names exactly that file in the content's own tree, because a sync that wants the save must carry the image.

data.files_established_for: content loaded as a single .d88 image. With the option on, every sector write lands in the loaded image itself — the save is the modified content file, no file of the core's own appears anywhere. An .m3u playlist's member images take the writes instead of the playlist, and anything the built-in menu opens takes its own
data.citation: src/LIBRETRO/file-op.c:441-445 at libretro/quasi88-libretro 42be798 — with the diff off the write falls through to the plain write on the opened image; the core accepts only d88 and m3u content (libretro.c:742)
